On the optimization side, most of my hands-on work has been in machine learning: gradient-boosted models on a roughly 10 million record survey dataset, a CNN trained in PyTorch to about 95% PCK for facial landmark prediction, and a learning-to-rank layer for alert prioritization in the anomaly-detection system I work on now. I've also worked close to hardware and sensor data, programming a microcontroller-based dust sensor in C/C++ and building a passive sleep-estimation system from Core Motion signals like gait speed and movement patterns. I have not taken formal motion planning or control theory coursework yet. That's the gap I'd be closing in this internship, and I learn fastest by building against a real system with real failure modes.

fields.expected:
Honestly, I don't have a robotics project to point to here. The closest hardware work I've done is programming a microcontroller-based dust sensor in C/C++ for my Valley Fever research, alongside an SIR-style model I built in Python from the differential equations, and I'd be overstating things to call that robotics.

Where I can speak to failure is in software that touches the real world. Building my Playwright job-application agent, the thing that kept biting me was that a capability passing a local fixture told me almost nothing about whether it worked against a live page. So I stopped trusting green tests and built an explicit validation ladder: UNIT_CONFIRMED, FIXTURE_CONFIRMED, LIVE_READ_ONLY_CONFIRMED, LIVE_MUTATION_CONFIRMED. Nothing gets called working until it has been validated at the level of reality it claims to support, and every mutating action sits behind a fail-closed flag so a bug can't quietly do something irreversible.

I expect manipulation to punish simulation-only confidence in the same way, and that's the part I want to learn firsthand.

fields.expected:
No. I have not worked with robotic manipulators, end-effectors, or custom test rigs, and I don't want to stretch what I've done into something it isn't.

The only physical hardware I've built with is a microcontroller-based dust sensor I programmed in C/C++ for my Valley Fever research. That work was about getting real environmental readings into a model: I built an SIR-style epidemiological model in Python from its differential equations and connected the disease dynamics to environmental variables related to dust and agriculture. The hard part for me was less the physical assembly than trusting the signal, since a sensor reading that looks plausible but is wrong quietly corrupts everything downstream.

The closest thing to sensor calibration in my more recent work is the passive sleep-estimation system I built for ClarityAtlas, using HealthKit and Core Motion signals like step count, gait speed, and movement patterns to infer sleep without a wearable, then validating that inference against real users in a Hopkins pilot with 30+ people.

I'd be starting from zero on physical manipulation setups, and I'd rather say that plainly.
